danish.title: Femtende bog (1812–13) — Kapitel 10
paragraphs: Den franske hær smeltede bort med en matematisk progressions regelmæssighed; og overgangen over Berezina, som der er skrevet så meget om, var blot ét mellemliggende trin i dens ødelæggelse og slet ikke felttogets afgørende begivenhed. Grunden til, at der er og stadig bliver skrevet så meget om Berezina, er fra fransk side, at de ulykker, hæren hidtil havde lidt, pludselig ved den ødelagte bro over floden blev samlet i ét tragisk skuespil, der brændte sig fast i alles erindring; og fra russisk side blot, at der i Petersborg — langt fra krigsscenen — var blevet udtænkt en plan (endnu en af Pfuels) til at fange Napoleon i en strategisk fælde ved Berezina. Alle forsikrede hinanden om, at alt ville ske efter planen, og insisterede derfor på, at netop overgangen over Berezina ødelagde den franske hær. I virkeligheden var resultaterne af overgangen langt mindre katastrofale for franskmændene — i tabte kanoner og mænd — end Krasnoje havde været, som tallene viser.

Berezina-overgangens eneste betydning ligger i det forhold, at den klart og uimodsigeligt beviste fejlagtigheden i alle planer om at afskære fjendens tilbagetog og rigtigheden af den eneste mulige handlemåde — den, som Kutuzov og hærens brede masse krævede — nemlig simpelthen at følge fjenden. Den franske folkemængde flygtede med stadigt stigende fart, og al dens energi var rettet mod at nå sit mål. Den flygtede som et såret dyr, og det var umuligt at spærre dens vej. Dette viste sig ikke så meget i de foranstaltninger, der blev truffet til overgangen, som i det, der skete ved broerne. Da broerne brød sammen, kastede ubevæbnede soldater, folk fra Moskva og kvinder med børn, der fulgte den franske tros, sig alle — drevet af træghedslov — ud i bådene og det isdækkede vand og overgav sig ikke.

Den drift var fornuftig. Forholdene for flygtninge og forfølgere var lige dårlige. Så længe man blev hos sine egne, kunne man håbe på hjælp fra kammeraterne og den faste plads, man indtog blandt dem. Men de, der overgav sig, ville, skønt de forblev i den samme ynkelige tilstand, stå lavere, når de nødvendige livsfornødenheder skulle fordeles. Franskmændene behøvede ikke at blive fortalt, at halvdelen af fangerne — som russerne ikke vidste, hvad de skulle stille op med — omkom af kulde og sult trods fangevogternes ønske om at redde dem; de følte, at det ikke kunne være anderledes. De mest medfølende russiske befalingsmænd, de der var venligt stemt over for franskmændene — og selv franskmændene i russisk tjeneste — kunne intet gøre for fangerne. Franskmændene omkom under de selvsamme forhold, som den russiske hær selv var udsat for. Det var umuligt at tage brød og tøj fra vores sultne og uundværlige soldater for at give det til franskmænd, der ganske vist ikke var skadelige, hadede eller skyldige, men simpelthen overflødige. Nogle russere gjorde det alligevel, men de var undtagelser.
Sikker undergang lå bag franskmændene, men foran lå håb. Deres skibe var brændt, der var ingen frelse uden kollektiv flugt, og herpå blev al den franske styrke samlet.

Jo længere de flygtede, desto mere elendig blev den tilbageblevne floks skæbne, især efter Berezina, som russerne (som følge af Petersborg-planen) havde knyttet særlige forhåbninger til, og desto skarpere blev de russiske befalingsmænds lidenskaber, idet de gav hinanden og frem for alt Kutuzov skylden. Forventningen om, at fiaskoen med Petersborg-Berezina-planen ville blive tilskrevet Kutuzov, førte til utilfredshed, foragt og hån, der blev udtrykt stadigt stærkere. Hånen og foragten blev naturligvis formuleret i respektfulde vendinger, der gjorde det umuligt for ham at spørge, hvori han fejlede. De talte ikke alvorligt til ham; når de rapporterede eller bad om hans sanktion, lod de som om de opfyldte en beklagelig formalitet, men de blinkede bag hans ryg og forsøgte at føre ham bag lyset ved enhver lejlighed.

Fordi de ikke kunne forstå ham, antog alle disse mennesker, at det var nytteløst at tale med den gamle mand; at han aldrig ville fatte dybden i deres planer, at han ville svare med sine talemåder (som de anså for tomme ord) om en »gylden bro«, om det umulige i at krydse grænsen med en flok pjaltede stakler og så videre. De havde hørt det hele før. Og alt, hvad han sagde — at man måtte afvente forsyninger, eller at soldaterne ikke havde støvler — var så enkelt, mens det, de foreslog, var så kompliceret og snedigt, at det var indlysende, at han var gammel og dum, og at de, skønt de ikke sad på magten, var geniale hærførere.

Efter foreningen med hæren under den glimrende admiral og Petersborg-helt Wittgenstein nåede denne stemning og stabens sladder sit højdepunkt. Kutuzov så det og sukkede blot og trak på skuldrene. Kun én gang, efter affæren ved Berezina, blev han vred og skrev følgende brev til Bennigsen (Bennigsen), der rapporterede direkte til kejseren:
»På grund af Deres gentagne sygemeldinger vil Deres Excellence behage at begive Dem til Kaluga ved modtagelsen af dette og dér afvente yderligere ordrer og udnævnelser fra Hans Kejserlige Majestæt.«

Men efter Bennigsens afgang sluttede storfyrst-tronfølgeren Konstantin Pavlovitj sig til hæren. Han havde deltaget i felttogets begyndelse, men var efterfølgende blevet fjernet fra hæren af Kutuzov. Nu, da han var kommet til hæren, meddelte han Kutuzov kejserens mishag med de ringe fremskridt og den langsomme fremrykning. Kejseren agtede selv at slutte sig til hæren om få dage.

Den gamle mand, erfaren i hoffets såvel som i militære anliggender — den samme Kutuzov, der i august var blevet valgt til øverstkommanderende mod kejserens ønske, og som havde fjernet storfyrsten og tronfølgeren fra hæren — som på eget ansvar og i modstrid med kejserens vilje havde besluttet at opgive Moskva — indså nu øjeblikkeligt, at hans tid var omme, at hans rolle var udspillet, og at den magt, han formodedes at sidde inde med, ikke længere var hans. Og han forstod det ikke blot af hoffets holdning. Han så på den ene side, at den militære opgave, hvori han havde spillet sin rolle, var forbi, og følte, at hans mission var fuldbragt; og på den anden side begyndte han at mærke sin aldrende krops fysiske træthed og behovet for hvile.

Den niogtyvende november drog Kutuzov ind i Vilna — hans »kære Vilna«, som han kaldte den. To gange i sin karriere havde Kutuzov været guvernør i Vilna. I den velhavende by, der ikke var blevet beskadiget, fandt han gamle venner og forbindelser foruden de bekvemmeligheder, han så længe havde måttet undvære. Og han vendte sig pludselig fra hærens og statens anliggender og fordybede sig, så vidt lidenskaberne omkring ham tillod det, i det rolige liv, han tidligere havde været vant til, som om alt det, der skete, og alt det, der endnu restede at gøre i historiens rige, slet ikke vedkom ham.

Tjitjagov, en af de mest ivrige »afskærere« og »opsplittere«, der først havde villet foretage en diversion i Grækenland og derefter i Warszawa, men aldrig ønskede at tage derhen, hvor han blev sendt — Tjitjagov, der var kendt for den dristighed, hvormed han talte til kejseren, og som mente, at Kutuzov stod i gæld til ham, fordi han, da han i 1811 blev sendt for at slutte fred med Tyrkiet uafhængigt af Kutuzov og fandt, at freden allerede var sluttet, indrømmede over for kejseren, at æren for freden i virkeligheden tilkom Kutuzov — denne Tjitjagov var den første til at møde Kutuzov på slottet, hvor sidstnævnte skulle bo. I marineuniform uden gallatøj, med dolk og kasket under armen overrakte han Kutuzov en garnisonsrapport og byens nøgler. Den foragteligt respektfulde holdning fra de yngre mænd over for den gamle i hans affældighed kom til sit stærkeste udtryk i Tjitjagovs opførsel, som kendte til de beskyldninger, der rettedes mod Kutuzov.
Da Kutuzov talte med Tjitjagov, nævnte han i forbifarten, at de vogne med porcelæn, der var blevet taget fra ham i Borisov, var genvundet og ville blive tilbageleveret.

»De vil antyde, at jeg ikke har noget at spise af.... Tværtimod, jeg kan forsyne Dem med alt, selv om De ønsker at holde middagsselskaber,« svarede Tjitjagov heftigt, idet han ved hvert ord forsøgte at bevise sin egen retskaffenhed og derfor forestillede sig, at Kutuzov var drevet af det samme ønske.
Kutuzov trak på skuldrene og svarede med sit subtile, gennemtrængende smil: »Jeg mente blot at sige, hvad jeg sagde.«

Imod kejserens ønske tilbageholdt Kutuzov størstedelen af hæren i Vilna. De omkring ham sagde, at han blev usædvanlig slap og fysisk svækket under sit ophold i byen. Han tog sig modstræbende af hærens anliggender, overlod alt til sine generaler, og mens han afventede kejserens ankomst, førte han et udsvævende levned.

Kejseren forlod Petersborg den syvende december med sit følge — grev Tolstoj, fyrst Volkonskij, Araktjejev og andre — og nåede Vilna den ellevte, hvor han i sin rejseslæde kørte direkte til slottet. Trods den strenge frost stod et hundrede generaler og stabsofficerer i fuld galauniform foran slottet tillige med en æresvagt fra Semjonov-regimentet.

En kurer, der galopperede foran til slottet i en trojka med tre skumsprøjtende heste, råbte »Han kommer!«, og Konovnitsyn styrtede ind i vestibulen for at underrette Kutuzov, der ventede i portnerlogen.

Et minut senere vaklede den gamle mands store, svære skikkelse i gallauniform, brystet dækket af ordener og et skærf trukket om maven, ud på trappen. Han satte sin hat på med de to spidser til siderne, og med handskerne i hånden og med besvær gående sidelæns ned ad trappetrinene til gadeniveau tog han den rapport, han havde forberedt til kejseren, i hånden.

Der løb folk frem og tilbage og hviskedes; endnu en trojka susede voldsomt op, og så rettede alle blikke sig mod en nærmende slæde, hvori man allerede kunne skimte kejserens og Volkonskijs skikkelser.

Af halvtreds års vane havde alt dette en fysisk ophidsende virkning på den gamle general. Han følte omhyggeligt og hastigt over sig selv, rettede på hatten, og idet han strammede sig op og rettede sig, rakte han i netop det øjeblik, da kejseren steg ud af slæden og løftede blikket mod ham, rapporten frem og begyndte at tale med sin bløde, indsmigrende stemme.

Kejseren skannede med et hurtigt blik Kutuzov fra top til tå, rynkede panden et øjeblik, men beherskede sig straks, gik hen til den gamle mand, strakte armene ud og omfavnede ham. Og også denne omfavnelse — på grund af et gammelt og dybtliggende indtryk forbundet med hans inderste følelser — havde sin sædvanlige virkning på Kutuzov, og han kom til at hulke.
Kejseren hilste på officererne og Semjonov-garden og trykkede atter den gamle mands hånd, mens de gik ind på slottet.

Da kejseren var alene med feltmarskalken, udtrykte han sin utilfredshed med forfølgelsens langsommelighed og med fejlene ved Krasnoje og Berezina og meddelte sine planer for et fremtidigt felttog i udlandet. Kutuzov afgav hverken indvending eller bemærkning. Det samme underdanige, udtryksløse blik, hvormed han havde lyttet til kejserens ordrer på slagmarken ved Austerlitz syv år tidligere, lagde sig over hans ansigt nu.
Da Kutuzov kom ud af studereværelset og med sænket hoved krydsede balsalen med sin tunge, vuggende gang, blev han standset af nogens stemme, der sagde:
»Deres Durchlaucht!«
Kutuzov løftede hovedet og så længe ind i øjnene på grev Tolstoj, der stod foran ham med et sølvfad, hvorpå der lå en lille genstand. Kutuzov syntes ikke at forstå, hvad der forventedes af ham.

Pludselig lod han til at huske; et knap mærkbart smil gled over hans opsvulmede ansigt, og idet han bøjede sig dybt og ærbødigt, tog han den genstand, der lå på fadet. Det var Sankt Georgs-ordenen af Første Klasse.

english.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: The French army melted away at the steady rate of a mathematical progression, and the crossing of the Berezina—about which so much has been written—was only one intermediate stage in its destruction, not at all the decisive episode of the campaign. If so much has been and still is written about the Berezina, on the French side this is only because at the broken bridge across that river, the calamities the army had been enduring were suddenly concentrated into a single tragic spectacle that seared itself into every memory. On the Russian side, it's simply because in Petersburg—far from the actual fighting—yet another plan (one of Pfuel's) had been devised to trap Napoleon at the Berezina River. Everyone was certain that everything would go according to plan, and therefore insisted that it was the Berezina crossing that destroyed the French army. In reality, the results of the crossing were far less disastrous to the French—in guns and men lost—than Krasnoe had been, as the numbers show.

The sole importance of the Berezina crossing lies in the fact that it plainly and undeniably proved the bankruptcy of all the plans to cut off the enemy's retreat, and confirmed the soundness of the only possible course of action—the one Kutuzov and the mass of the army demanded—which was simply to follow the enemy. The French mob fled at ever-increasing speed, all its energy directed toward reaching its goal. It fled like a wounded animal, and it was impossible to block its path. This was shown not so much by its arrangements for crossing as by what happened at the bridges. When the bridges collapsed, unarmed soldiers, civilians from Moscow, and women with children who were traveling with the French—all carried forward by sheer momentum—piled into boats and onto the ice-covered water and refused to surrender.

That impulse was entirely rational. The condition of both fugitives and pursuers was equally miserable. As long as they stayed with their own people, each could hope for help from comrades and hold a defined place among them. But those who surrendered, while remaining in the same wretched state, would drop to a lower level in any claim on the necessities of life. The French didn't need to be told that half the prisoners—whom the Russians didn't know what to do with—perished of cold and hunger despite their captors' desire to save them. They sensed it could not be otherwise. The most compassionate Russian commanders, those favorably disposed toward the French—even Frenchmen serving in the Russian army—could do nothing for the prisoners. The French perished from the very conditions to which the Russian army itself was exposed. It was impossible to take bread and clothing from starving, essential Russian soldiers to give to Frenchmen who, though not threatening or hated or guilty, were simply unnecessary. Some Russians even did that, but they were exceptions.

Certain destruction lay behind the French, but ahead lay hope. Their bridges had been burned; there was no salvation except in collective flight, and on that the whole strength of the French was concentrated.

The farther they fled, the more wretched became the plight of the remnant—especially after the Berezina, on which (thanks to the Petersburg plan) the Russians had placed such high hopes—and the more heated grew the passions of the Russian commanders, who blamed one another and above all Kutuzov. Anticipating that the failure of the Petersburg Berezina plan would be blamed on Kutuzov led to increasing dissatisfaction, contempt, and ridicule. The ridicule and contempt were expressed, of course, in respectful form, making it impossible for him to ask what exactly he was being accused of. They didn't talk seriously to him; when reporting or asking for his approval, they appeared to be fulfilling an unpleasant formality while winking behind his back and trying to undermine him at every turn.

Because they couldn't understand him, all these people assumed it was useless to talk to the old man; that he would never grasp the profundity of their plans; that he would answer with his stock phrases about a "golden bridge," the impossibility of crossing the frontier with a mob of ragged men, and so on. They had heard all that before. And everything he said—that they needed to wait for supplies, that the men had no boots—was so simple, while what they proposed was so complex and clever, that it was obvious he was a stupid old man while they, though not in command, were military geniuses.

After the junction with the army of the brilliant admiral and Petersburg hero Wittgenstein, this mood and staff gossip reached a peak. Kutuzov saw this and merely sighed and shrugged. Only once, after the affair at the Berezina, did he get angry and write the following letter to Bennigsen (who reported separately to the Emperor):

"On account of your frequent bouts of ill health, would Your Excellency kindly be so good as to proceed to Kaluga upon receipt of this, there to await further commands and appointments from His Imperial Majesty."

But after Bennigsen's departure, the Grand Duke Constantine Pavlovich joined the army. He had participated at the beginning of the campaign but had been removed by Kutuzov. Now, returning to the army, he informed Kutuzov of the Emperor's displeasure at the slow progress and poor results. The Emperor intended to join the army personally in a few days.

The old man, experienced in both court and military affairs—this same Kutuzov who in August had been chosen commander in chief against the sovereign's wishes, who had removed the Grand Duke and heir apparent from the army, who on his own authority and contrary to the Emperor's will had decided to abandon Moscow—now instantly understood that his day was over, his role played out, and the power he supposedly held was no longer his. And he understood this not merely from the court's attitude. He saw, on the one hand, that the military campaign in which he had played his part was finished, and he felt his mission was accomplished. At the same time, he began to feel the physical weariness of his aged body and the need for rest.

On November twenty-ninth, Kutuzov entered Vilna—his "dear Vilna," as he called it. Twice during his career he had been governor of Vilna. In that wealthy city, which had not been damaged, he found old friends and associations as well as the comforts of life he had so long been deprived of. And he suddenly turned from the cares of army and state, and as far as the passions seething around him allowed, immersed himself in the quiet life he had once known, as if everything happening in the world of history no longer concerned him at all.

Chichagov—one of the most zealous proponents of "cutting off" and "breaking through," who had first wanted to operate in Greece, then in Warsaw, but never wished to go where he was actually sent; Chichagov, noted for his bold manner of speaking to the Emperor, and who considered Kutuzov indebted to him (because when he was sent to conclude peace with Turkey in 1811, independently of Kutuzov, he found the peace already made and acknowledged to the Emperor that the credit belonged to Kutuzov)—this Chichagov was the first to meet Kutuzov at the castle where the latter was to stay. In undress naval uniform, carrying a dirk with his cap under his arm, he handed Kutuzov a garrison report and the keys to the city. The contemptuous-yet-respectful attitude of the younger generation toward the old man in his dotage was expressed to the highest degree in Chichagov's behavior, as he was well aware of the accusations being leveled at Kutuzov.
In conversation with Chichagov, Kutuzov happened to mention that the vehicles packed with china captured from him at Borisov had been recovered and would be returned.

"You mean to imply that I have nothing to eat from? On the contrary, I can supply you with everything, even if you want to throw dinner parties," Chichagov replied warmly, trying with every word to prove his own integrity and therefore imagining Kutuzov was driven by the same concern.
Kutuzov, shrugging his shoulders, replied with his subtle, knowing smile: "I merely meant what I said."

Contrary to the Emperor's wishes, Kutuzov kept the greater part of the army in Vilna. Those around him said he became extraordinarily slack and physically feeble during his stay. He attended to army business reluctantly, left everything to his generals, and while waiting for the Emperor to arrive led a leisurely life.

The Emperor left Petersburg on December seventh with his retinue—Count Tolstoy, Prince Volkonsky, Arakcheev, and others—and reached Vilna on the eleventh. In his traveling sleigh, he drove straight to the castle. Despite the severe frost, about a hundred generals and staff officers in full dress uniform stood before the castle, along with a guard of honor from the Semenov regiment.
A courier galloping ahead in a troika with three foam-flecked horses shouted "Coming!" and Konovnitsyn rushed into the vestibule to inform Kutuzov, who was waiting in the porter's lodge.

A minute later, the old man's large, heavy figure in full-dress uniform—his chest covered with medals and a sash wrapped around his stomach—waddled out onto the porch. He put on his two-pointed hat, and holding his gloves in one hand, walked with effort sideways down the steps to street level, taking in his other hand the report he had prepared for the Emperor.

There was running to and fro and whispering; another troika flew up at great speed, and then all eyes turned to an approaching sleigh in which the figures of the Emperor and Volkonsky could already be seen.

From the force of fifty years' habit, all this had a physically exciting effect on the old general. He carefully felt himself all over, adjusted his hat, and pulling himself together, drew himself upright. At the very moment the Emperor stepped down from the sleigh and looked up at him, Kutuzov handed over the report and began speaking in his smooth, ingratiating voice.

The Emperor swept a rapid glance over Kutuzov from head to foot, frowned for an instant, but immediately composed himself, stepped forward, extended his arms, and embraced the old man. This embrace too, because of a deep-seated emotional association, had its usual effect on Kutuzov, and he gave a sob.
The Emperor greeted the officers and the Semenov guard, then pressed the old man's hand again and went into the castle with him.

When alone with the field marshal, the Emperor expressed his dissatisfaction at the slowness of the pursuit and the mistakes made at Krasnoe and the Berezina, and outlined his plans for a future campaign abroad. Kutuzov made no objection or comment. The same submissive, expressionless look with which he had listened to the Emperor's orders on the field of Austerlitz seven years before settled on his face.
When Kutuzov came out of the study and was crossing the ballroom with his heavy, waddling gait, head bowed, someone's voice stopped him:
"Your Serene Highness!"

Kutuzov raised his head and looked for a long time into the eyes of Count Tolstoy, who stood before him holding a silver tray on which lay a small object. Kutuzov seemed not to understand what was expected of him.

Suddenly he appeared to remember. A barely perceptible smile flickered across his puffy face, and bowing low and respectfully, he took the object from the tray. It was the Order of St. George, First Class.
